Numerical Investigation of Multiphase Helium Flow and Entropy Generation in a Joule Thomson Valve

Seminar Type:

Prof. S Datta (PIC, Departmental Seminar)

Abstract:

Joule-Thomson (JT) cryocoolers are widely used in compact and spaceborne cryogenic systems due to their simplicity, reliability, and absence of moving parts in the cold region. The throttle valve induces a large pressure drop and partial liquefaction of helium, resulting in complex multiphase flow. Understanding the flow structure and thermodynamic irreversibilities is essential for improving cooling performance. In this study, multiphase helium flow through a micro-JT throttle valve is numerically investigated using a compressible multiphase mixture model with real gas thermophysical properties. Flow-field analysis and second law-based entropy generation analysis quantify irreversibilities caused by viscous dissipation and thermal conduction. The influence of orifice length on flow structure, phase distribution, and entropy generation is systematically examined. Rapid expansion produces strong flow acceleration and a distinct liquid vapor mixture region downstream of the orifice, whose size and strength vary with orifice length. Longer orifices increase viscous dissipation and internal entropy generation, whereas shorter orifices shift dominant irreversibilities downstream. The results indicate an optimal orifice length that minimizes total entropy generation while maintaining the required pressure drop and cooling effect. These findings provide physical insights and design guidelines for optimizing miniature JT valves for high-performance cryogenic applications.
